Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 112, verses 1–4:

We begin this session with the words of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One (1) Allah, the Eternal Refuge (2)﴾ [al-Ikhlas 1, 2], and what is easy of the two surahs after it.

Allah, blessed and exalted is He, says to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One﴾. This address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to the Ummah as well.

As for ﴿He is Allah, the One﴾: ﴿He﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) according to the grammarians (al-mu'rabūn, those who analyse the i'rab, grammatical case endings), and the word of majesty ﴿Allah﴾ is the predicate of the subject[[This follows the view that ﴿He﴾ is a subject whose first predicate is the proper name ﴿Allah﴾ and whose second predicate is ﴿One﴾. If we parse ﴿He﴾ as the pronoun of the matter, then the name ﴿Allah﴾ is a second subject, ﴿One﴾ is the predicate of the second subject, and the sentence ﴿Allah, the One﴾ is the predicate of the first subject, which is the pronoun of the matter.]], and ﴿One﴾ is a second predicate, and ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is an independent sentence.

They mention concerning the occasion of revelation of this surah that "the polytheists or the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Describe your Lord to us, of what is He made? So Allah revealed this surah."[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (606) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

﴿Say, He is Allah﴾, meaning: He is Allah, the One you speak of and ask about. ﴿One﴾, meaning: He is singular in His majesty and greatness, He has no equal, and He has no partner; rather, He is unique in majesty and greatness, may He be mighty and majestic.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ is an independent sentence in which Allah, exalted is He, makes clear that He is ﴿the Eternal Refuge﴾. So what is the meaning of ﴿al-Samad﴾?

The most comprehensive of what has been said about its meaning is that it is the One perfect in His attributes, the One to whom all His creatures turn in need. It has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that "al-Samad is the One perfect in His knowledge, perfect in His forbearance, perfect in His might, perfect in His power," and so on to the end of what is mentioned in the report.[[Ibn Jarir reported in his tafsir (24/692) with his chain from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿al-Samad﴾: "He says: the Lord who has become perfect in His lordship, the noble who has become perfect in His nobility, the great who has become great in His greatness, the forbearing who has become perfect in His forbearance, the self-sufficient who has become perfect in His self-sufficiency, the mighty who has become perfect in His dominion, the knowing who has become perfect in His knowledge, the wise who has become perfect in His wisdom; and He is the One who is perfect in all kinds of nobility and lordship; He is Allah, glorified is He; this is His attribute, which befits none but Him."]] This means that He is free of need from all creatures, because He is perfect. It is also reported in its interpretation that al-Samad is the One to whom creation turns in its needs, and this means that all creatures are in need of Him. Accordingly, the comprehensive meaning of al-Samad is: the One perfect in His attributes, to whom all His creatures turn in need.

﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas 3]. ﴿He neither begets﴾, because He, majestic and exalted, has no equal, and a child is derived from his father and is a part of him; as the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning Fatimah: "She is a part of me."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (3714) and Muslim (2449/94), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Fatimah is a part of me; whoever angers her angers me."]] And Allah, majestic and exalted is He, has no equal. Furthermore, a child is only had out of need for it: either for help in bearing the hardships of the world, or out of need for the continuation of offspring; and Allah, mighty and majestic, is free of all that. Therefore ﴿He does not beget﴾, because He has no equal, and because He is free of need from everyone, mighty and majestic.

Allah, mighty and majestic, has also indicated the impossibility of His having offspring in His saying: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no companion and He created all things, and He is Knowing of all things?﴾ [al-An'am 101]. A child requires a spouse to bear it, and likewise He is the Creator of everything; so if He is the Creator of everything, then everything is separate from Him and distinct from Him.

﴿And He is not begotten﴾, because He, mighty and majestic, is the First, before whom there is nothing. How could He be begotten?!

In this last sentence there is a refutation of three deviant groups among the children of Adam: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians. The polytheists made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, female, and said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. The Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah. The Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah. Allah refuted them with His saying: ﴿He neither begets﴾. So His saying ﴿He neither begets﴾ contains a refutation of three groups — and I had made this the last, but the correct view is the first — ﴿He neither begets﴾ is a refutation of three groups of the children of Adam, all of them astray: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians; because the polytheists say the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Christians say the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the Jews say 'Uzayr is the son of Allah.

﴿And He is not begotten﴾, because He is the First, before whom there is nothing.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him, (none) equal to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas 4], meaning: no one is equal to Him in all His attributes. Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, negated for Himself that He is a begetter, or begotten, or has an equal.

This surah has great merit. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is equal to one third of the Quran,"[[Reported by al-Bukhari (5013) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Muslim (811/259) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.]] but it is equal to it and does not take its place; it equals one third of the Quran but does not substitute for one third of the Quran. The proof is that if a person repeated it three times in an obligatory prayer, it would not suffice him in place of al-Fatihah, even though if he recites it three times it is as if he recited the whole Quran. But it does not suffice in its place. Do not be surprised that a thing may be equal to another thing without being a substitute for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that "whoever says: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things capable,"[[Reported by Muslim (2693/30) with his chain from the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him) from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever says: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things capable, ten times, it is as if he had freed four souls from the descendants of Isma'il."]] — and yet if he had a neck (slave) owed as expiation and he said this remembrance, it would not suffice him from the expiation. So equality of one thing with another does not necessarily mean that it stands in its place regarding sufficiency.

The Messenger (ﷺ) used to recite this surah in the second rak'ah of the Fajr sunnah, in the sunnah of Maghrib, in the two rak'ahs of tawaf, and likewise he recited it in the third rak'ah of witr; because it is founded on pure sincerity (ikhlas) to Allah, and for this reason it is called Surat al-Ikhlas.

In this last sentence there is a refutation of three deviant groups among the children of Adam: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians. The polytheists made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, female, and said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. The Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah. The Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah. Allah refuted them with His saying: ﴿He neither begets﴾. So His saying ﴿He neither begets﴾ contains a refutation of three groups — and I had made this the last, but the correct view is the first — ﴿He neither begets﴾ is a refutation of three groups of the children of Adam, all of them astray: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians; because the polytheists say the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Christians say the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the Jews say 'Uzayr is the son of Allah.

﴿And He is not begotten﴾, because He is the First, before whom there is nothing.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him, (none) equal to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas 4], meaning: no one is equal to Him in all His attributes. Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, negated for Himself that He is a begetter, or begotten, or has an equal.

This surah has great merit. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is equal to one third of the Quran,"[[Reported by al-Bukhari (5013) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Muslim (811/259) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.]] but it is equal to it and does not take its place; it equals one third of the Quran but does not substitute for one third of the Quran. The proof is that if a person repeated it three times in an obligatory prayer, it would not suffice him in place of al-Fatihah, even though if he recites it three times it is as if he recited the whole Quran. But it does not suffice in its place. Do not be surprised that a thing may be equal to another thing without being a substitute for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that "whoever says: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things capable,"[[Reported by Muslim (2693/30) with his chain from the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him) from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever says: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise, and He is over all things capable, ten times, it is as if he had freed four souls from the descendants of Isma'il."]] — and yet if he had a neck (slave) owed as expiation and he said this remembrance, it would not suffice him from the expiation. So equality of one thing with another does not necessarily mean that it stands in its place regarding sufficiency.

The Messenger (ﷺ) used to recite this surah in the second rak'ah of the Fajr sunnah, in the sunnah of Maghrib, in the two rak'ahs of tawaf, and likewise he recited it in the third rak'ah of witr; because it is founded on pure sincerity (ikhlas) to Allah, and for this reason it is called Surat al-Ikhlas.
